8. The learned Advocate on both sides, have taken me through the judgment of the courts below and also the evidence on record. Mr. Dewan A.M.S. Zaman, the learned Advocate for the appellant, contends that the courts below committed an error of law in not taking into consideration the facts that the defendants claim title in the suit land since 1947 by defendant NO.1 and 1950 by the other defendants and they have acquired title by adverse possession in the suit land even before the auction sale took place on 4.1.64. Mr. Zaman further contends that-the learned Additional District Judge misread the evidence of defendants and observed that defendant No. 1 demolished his case when he stated in cross that he constructed huts in the suitland 8/9 years back. But as a matter of fact defendant No. 1 stated that he purchased the house 23 years back and since then lives there on payment of taxes ctc, constructed two huts 7/8 years back. From a perusal of the deposition of D.W. 1 (Deft No.1) it seems that he claimed to have been living in the suit homestead since his purchase 23 years ago. The learned Additional District Judge with reference to the possession of the sui t land by the defendant observed as follows: "Deft. No. I is said to have taken possession of the suit land in 1344 B.S. that means long 17 years back, but he has demolished this story by Slating in cross exam inaction that he created his hut on the disputed homestead 8/9 years back, that means in or about the time of the auction sale which tallies with the puffs’, case. Defendants 3 & 7 are said to have gone into possession in 1356 B.S. corresponding to 1949. But D.W. 2 Akram Ullah has demolished their case by stating that after their migration to Calcutta in 1947 the original owners never came back to this pan or the country. This Ialsifics the story 01" having been inducted in possession in 1356 B.S. Had the defdts, been in possession of the suit land or parts thereof right frol11.1947 there was no reason for their such possession being not recorded in the S.S. Khatian which operation continued from 1954 to 1962. D.W. 3 contesting defdt No.3 himself demolished his own case by stating in contradiction to his writ- ten statement case that he purchased this suit- land in 1326 B.S. This cuts at the very root of the defence case. Story of adverse possession cannot be believed on the basis of such inconsistent and contradictory statements of witnesses. Extinction of title of a legal owner must be on the basis of most satisfactory evidence. In the instant case. there is even no touch of genuineness in the case of the contesting defdts. and upon careful scrutiny of the evidence on record I am left with the only .impression that the defdts. have trespassed into the suit land during the certificate sale proceedings as alleged in the plaint and thereafter they have fabricated some documents in their auempi to grab the property." 

 9. It is admitted that the suitland belonged to Sarada Ranjan De and Kumud Ranjan De both of whom migrated to India. Defence case is that they left lor India in 1947, selling 442 acres of land to the defendant No.1 and putting him in charge of other property and they sold the remaining portion of the suitland 10 the other defendants in 1950 ami since I ()n and 1950 the defendants arc in possession of the suitland. The defendant's possession in the suit land including the homestead is not denied. Rather it is admitted. as the plaintiff wants khas possession by evicting the defendants from the same. Now the question is from which time the defendants are in possession. The courts below seems to have held that the defendants trespassed into and came in position of the suitland only about the time or the auction sale. But from the evidence on records, this finding of the courts below, is not supported. There is no evidence to hold that Kumud Ranjan and Sarada Ranjan De were in possession of the suitland at the time. the auction sale took place. From the certified copy of the order sheet of Certificate Case No. ()244 of 1962-63 which is marked Ext 0(1), it appears that the notices under section 7 of the Public Demands Recovery Act returned unnerved with the report that certificate-debtors were living in India in July 1963. ThisExt D (1) thus supports the defence case that the certificate-debtors were not in the then East Pakistan and they left for India, according to the defendants in 1947. Further the case of the defence is that the defendant-appellant paid rent for the suitland and got the rent receipt and he also sent rent by Money Order for the years for which arrear of rents the property was put on auction sale, at the instance of plain- tiff. 

 10. Mr. Zaman, the learned Advocate for the appellant, contends that the defendants acquired title.in- the suitland by adverse possession-sinccJ9J7and1950 respectively and the judgment-debtors had no interest in the suitland when the auction sale held in1964 and as such, the plaintiff did not acquire any tile and interest. in the suitand and is not entitled to get any decree for the same. 

 11. Mr. B.K. Das, the learned Advocate for the respondents, contends that the defendants did not make any case of adverse possession in the written statement and in the courts below and as such, they cannot make out a new case here in the second appeal. But from the observation of the learned Additional District Judge quoted above, it appears that a case of adverse possession was argued before him but he did not accept that argument, as he did not believe the defence story of possession from 1947 & 1950 respectively. It is no doubt true that there is no satisfactory evidence by any independent witness about defence story of possession from 1947 and 1950 hut nevertheless there is no evidence to show that the certificate-debtors or any other persons except defenders were in possession of the suit and prior to the auction-purchase by the plaintiff. The plaintiff did not adduce any evidence to prove the claim of possession or the judgment-debtors in the suit and since 1947 and 1950 till the auction-sale in 1964. It appears that the courts below did not consider the defence story of possession from the proper angle and were under a wrong impression that the defendants jumped upon the suit and at about or after the auction purchase by the plaintiff. This wrong ingression of the courts below seems to have vitiated the decision arrived at by them. The decision seems To be erroneous and not based on evidence or proper consideration of the evidence in the proper perspective in the facts and circumstances of the case. 

 12. If the defendants are found to be in possession of the suit from 1947 and 1950 then the question as to whether they have acquired title by adverse possession against the certificate-debtors before the sale took place on 4.1.64, is to be considered. But the courts below did not consider that aspect.
